questions.q: A topic holds account balance updates keyed by account ID, where each new record replaces the account's previous balance. Which Kafka Streams abstraction models it?

options.t: KStream, because each record is an independent event
options.why: A KStream treats every record as an insert, so old balances would never be replaced.

options.t: KTable
A windowed KStream with one-minute tumbling windows
options.why: Windowing groups records by time; it doesn't turn updates into the latest value per key.

options.t: A KGroupedStream, read straight from the topic
options.why: A KGroupedStream comes from grouping a KStream; it isn't read from a topic.

questions.explain: A KTable is a changelog stream: each record is an update (upsert) for its key, so it holds the latest balance per account. A KStream treats each record as a self-contained insert.

questions.q: In a KTable, what does a record with a key and a null value mean?

options.t: A record to skip, because null values are invalid input
options.why: Null values are meaningful in a KTable.

options.t: An instruction to keep the previous value and ignore this one
options.why: It removes the key rather than keeping it.

options.t: A delete of that key
A marker that starts a new window for the key
options.why: KTables aren't windowed by nulls.

questions.explain: In a KTable each record is an update, and a null value is a delete (tombstone) for its key.

questions.q: An application enriches a high-volume stream of orders with a small, rarely changing product catalogue topic that has a different partition count. Which abstraction for the catalogue avoids a co-partitioning requirement?

options.t: GlobalKTable
KTable, after calling selectKey on the catalogue
options.why: A KTable join still needs co-partitioned inputs.

options.t: KStream, joined with a 1-hour window
options.why: A stream-stream join also needs co-partitioning.

options.t: A repartition of the orders topic to match the catalogue
options.why: That is how to make inputs co-partitioned, not how to avoid the requirement.

questions.explain: A GlobalKTable is populated with all partitions of its topic on every instance, so joins against it don't need co-partitioning, at the cost of more local storage.

questions.q: A stream keyed by customer ID needs each value converted from JSON text to an object, keeping the key, before a `groupByKey().count()`. Which operation avoids an unnecessary repartition?

options.t: map, returning the same key and the new value
options.why: map can change the key, so Kafka Streams marks the stream for repartitioning.

options.t: selectKey followed by map
options.why: selectKey marks the stream for repartitioning.

options.t: flatMap that returns a single key-value pair
options.why: flatMap can change the key, so it also marks the stream for repartitioning.

options.t: mapValues

questions.explain: `mapValues` and `flatMapValues` never cause repartitioning. `map`, `flatMap` and `selectKey` can change the key, so a later grouping or join repartitions.

questions.q: What is the difference between `groupBy` and `groupByKey` on a KStream?

options.t: groupBy always repartitions; groupByKey only if already marked
groupByKey always repartitions; groupBy never does
options.why: It's the other way round.

options.t: groupBy works only on KTables, and groupByKey only on KStreams
options.why: Both exist for KStreams.

options.t: There is none; they are aliases
options.why: groupBy selects a new key, which needs repartitioning.

questions.explain: `groupBy` always repartitions, because it chooses a new key. `groupByKey` repartitions only if the stream was already marked for repartitioning by an earlier key-changing operation.

questions.q: A team needs the average order value per customer, from a stream of order amounts (Long). Which aggregation lets the result have a different type from the input values?

options.t: count
options.why: count returns the number of records, not a custom result.

options.t: reduce
options.why: reduce keeps the input value type.

options.t: aggregate
filter
options.why: filter is a stateless operation, not an aggregation.

questions.explain: `reduce` keeps the value type; `aggregate` allows the aggregate to have a different type (here a sum and a count to compute an average).

options.t: A KStream of counts, one per input record
options.why: An aggregation of a KStream yields a KTable.

options.t: A single Long for the whole stream
options.why: It counts per key, continuously.

options.t: A GlobalKTable replicated to every instance
options.why: Aggregations produce a KTable, not a GlobalKTable.

options.t: A KTable of counts per key

questions.explain: An aggregation of a KStream yields a KTable, updated as new (and out-of-order) records arrive.

questions.q: Which window type is fixed-size and non-overlapping, so each record belongs to exactly one window?

options.t: Hopping
options.why: Hopping windows can overlap, so a record can be in several.

options.t: Tumbling
Session
options.why: Session windows vary in size per key.

options.t: Sliding
options.why: Sliding windows are aligned to record timestamps and overlap.

questions.explain: Tumbling windows are fixed-size, non-overlapping and gap-less; a tumbling window is a hopping window whose advance equals its size.

questions.q: A hopping window has a size of 5 minutes and an advance of 1 minute. How many windows does one record belong to?

options.t: One
options.why: That is true of tumbling windows.

options.t: Two
options.why: With a 1-minute hop over 5 minutes, more windows overlap each moment.

options.t: Five
It depends on the record's key
options.why: Hopping windows are aligned to the epoch, not to keys.

questions.explain: Hopping windows are fixed-size and can overlap: with size 5 minutes and advance 1 minute, a new window starts every minute, so each moment is covered by five windows.

questions.q: An analytics team wants to group each user's clicks into visits that end after 30 minutes with no activity. Which window type fits?

options.t: Session windows with a 30-minute inactivity gap
Tumbling windows of 30 minutes
options.why: Tumbling windows cut at fixed times, not at gaps in activity.

options.t: Hopping windows of 30 minutes with a 1-minute hop
options.why: Hopping windows are fixed-size and overlap; they don't follow activity.

options.t: A grace period of 30 minutes on any window
options.why: A grace period accepts late records; it doesn't define sessions.

questions.explain: Session windows group periods of activity separated by a gap of inactivity, tracked per key, so their sizes vary. User behaviour analysis is their main use.

questions.q: A one-hour tumbling window from 09:00 to 10:00 has a grace period of 10 minutes. A record with a 09:55 timestamp arrives when stream time is 10:15. What happens to it?

options.t: It is counted in the 09:00-10:00 window
options.why: The window closed at 10:10, when its grace period ended.

options.t: It is counted in the 10:00-11:00 window instead
options.why: Records go to the window of their own timestamp, or are dropped.

options.t: The window reopens for it
options.why: A closed window doesn't reopen.

options.t: It is dropped as too late

questions.explain: The grace period bounds lateness: the 09:00-10:00 window accepts out-of-order records until 10:10, then closes, and later records for it are dropped.

questions.q: A windowed count updates its result many times as records arrive, but downstream wants one result per window. Which operation does that?

options.t: A longer grace period on the window
options.why: Grace allows later records; it doesn't stop intermediate updates.

options.t: suppress(Suppressed.untilWindowCloses(...))
Switching the count to reduce
options.why: reduce emits updates just as count does.

options.t: Setting commit.interval.ms to the window size
options.why: Committing less often isn't a guarantee of final results.

questions.explain: `suppress(Suppressed.untilWindowCloses(...))` holds a window's updates and emits only its final result once the window closes.

questions.q: Which statement about KStream-KStream joins is right?

options.t: They are never windowed
options.why: They are always windowed.

options.t: They support inner joins only
options.why: They support inner, left and outer joins.

options.t: They are always windowed
They need a GlobalKTable on one side
options.why: Both sides are streams.

questions.explain: KStream-KStream joins are always windowed joins, and they support inner, left and outer variants.

questions.q: A KStream of payments (12 partitions) is joined with a KTable of accounts (8 partitions), both keyed by account ID. What is the problem?

options.t: None, because both inputs are keyed by the same account ID
options.why: The same key isn't enough; the partition counts must match too.

options.t: KStream-KTable joins are not supported
options.why: They are supported, as inner and left joins.

options.t: The join must be windowed
options.why: Only KStream-KStream joins are windowed.

options.t: The inputs aren't co-partitioned: partition counts differ

questions.explain: Joins need co-partitioned inputs: the same number of partitions and the same partitioning strategy, so equal keys land in the same partition number. Only foreign-key and GlobalKTable joins are exempt.

questions.q: Which TWO join types support an outer join in the Kafka Streams DSL?

options.t: KStream-KStream
KStream-KTable
options.why: It supports inner and left only.

options.t: KTable-KTable
KStream-GlobalKTable
options.why: It supports inner and left only.

options.t: KTable-KTable foreign-key
options.why: It supports inner and left only.

questions.explain: KStream-KStream and KTable-KTable joins support inner, left and outer. KStream-KTable, KStream-GlobalKTable and foreign-key joins support inner and left.

questions.q: A stream is split with `split()` into branches for `EU` and `US` orders, with no default branch. What happens to an order from `APAC`?

options.t: It goes to both branches
options.why: Each record goes to at most one branch, the first that matches.

options.t: It goes to the last branch
options.why: Branches don't catch unmatched records.

options.t: It is dropped
It stops the application with an exception
options.why: Unmatched records are dropped quietly when there is no default branch.

questions.explain: Each record goes to the first branch whose predicate matches; unmatched records go to the default branch, or are dropped if none was created.

questions.q: What is `application.id` used for in Kafka Streams?

options.t: Only as a label that appears in the application's own log lines
options.why: It drives the group ID, internal topic names and more.

options.t: The group ID, client ID prefix and internal topic prefix
The name of the output topic
options.why: Output topics are named in the topology.

options.t: The ID of the broker the application runs on
options.why: Applications don't run on brokers.

questions.explain: `application.id` (required, unique in the cluster) becomes the consumer group ID, the client ID prefix, the state directory subfolder and the prefix of internal topic names.

questions.q: A Streams application needs exactly-once processing. Which setting turns it on, and what changes with it by default?

options.t: enable.idempotence=true; nothing else changes
options.why: Streams uses processing.guarantee for exactly-once.

options.t: isolation.level=read_committed only
options.why: That's a consumer setting Streams manages for you under exactly-once.

options.t: processing.guarantee=exactly_once, which keeps a 30 s commit
options.why: The value is exactly_once_v2, and the commit interval drops to 100 ms.

options.t: processing.guarantee=exactly_once_v2; commits every 100 ms

questions.explain: `processing.guarantee` is `at_least_once` by default; `exactly_once_v2` turns on exactly-once, and `commit.interval.ms` then defaults to 100 instead of 30 000.
